newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: China top threat to Asian peace, experts say.
newsitem.headline: China top threat to Asian peace, experts say.

text.p: A resurgent China has become the main worry of Asia's strategic planners, two defence experts said on Wednesday.

"The first and core uncertainty pertains to the evolution of China into the future and the policies it will follow in Asia and the world," said Jasjit Singh, head of India's Institute for Defence Studies and Analyses.

"China's rapidly growing strength along with its demonstration and readiness to use assertive force, as the missile firings abeam Taiwan showed, are likely to generate a worse-case scenario in defence planning," he said in a speech prepared for delivery to a seminar in Singapore.
Shinichi Ogawa of Japan's National Institute of Defence Studies agreed.

"A rising power tends to be disruptive, if only because it is reluctant to accept international institutions and hierarchies of political prestige created when it was relatively weak," he said in a speech prepared for delivery.
And the "essentially incompatible" policies of economic openness and "repressive domestic rule" could have external consequences if the population became restive, Ogawa said.

"It might try to turn the population's eyes away from the increasingly difficult domestic issues by further instigating nationalism and irredentism. China does not lack territorial issues exploitable for that purpose," he said.

Both analysts said engaging China, not confronting it, was the answer to the potential problem, but Ogawa said that if China did carry out its threat to prevent Taiwanese independence by force, the effects would be tremendous.

"Taiwan is anything but an internal affair, since how the Taiwan issue unfolds has profound regional implications," he said of the island which China has regarded as a rebel province not entitled to foreign ties.

Both sides agree reunification is their aim, but differ on how to get there. Beijing says the issue is a purely internal one and has maintained a standing threat to recover the island by force if it opts for independence.

China launched a nine-month series of war games and missile tests off Taiwan after Taiwanese President Lee Teng-hui's private but high-profile visit to the United States in June 1995. The tests prompted Washington to send two aircraft carriers near the Taiwan strait to monitor the crisis during Taiwan's presidential election in March last year.
"Politically and morally, it would be hard for the democracies in Asia-Pacific, the United States in particular, to stand aside from the conflict," if China carried out its threat, Ogawa said.
But Mu Hui Min, secretary general of the China Institute for International Strategic Studies, said his country posed no threat.

"Her economic growth will pose no threat to any other countries but will make great contributions to peace and stability in the Asia-Pacific and the world," he said in a speech prepared for delivery to the seminar.
But he added: "Absolutely never can the whole of Chinese people agree with any attempt to split Taiwan from the motherland and fabricate independence of Taiwan."

Keynote speaker Jose T. Almonte of the Philippines National Security Council said there were potential problems with China and it was uncertain whether the country could complete its economic transformation "without mishap".
But Almonte said Asians could now hope trade and economic growth would conquer any potential for military conflict.
